newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China grain reform may remove farmers' safety net.
newsitem.headline: China grain reform may remove farmers' safety net.

text.p: China's plan to unify state grain purchase and market prices is probably aimed at saving the government money, but problems could arise if grain prices drop next year and hurt farmers, grain traders said on Thursday.

The Chinese government "has used a lot of money to build up grain reserves, they've actually lost a lot of money, if you compare where they bought and today's market price", said a senior grains trader in Singapore.
"It's an attempt to extricate the central government from some of these overall concerns," he said.

In a speech on Wednesday outlining some of Beijing's plans for reform in 1997 to drag China's economy away from Stalinist-style central planning and toward stronger market forces, Politburo member Li Tieying cited reform of lumbering state enterprises and agriculture as two primary objectives.

China would unify the grain purchasing prices with market prices next year, Li, the minister in charge of the State Commission for Restructuring the Economy, told a national conference on reform in the southern city of Shenzhen.
He gave no more details on how prices would be unified, but the move appeared to herald the effective liberalisation of grain prices.
Grain traders in Hong Kong and China said current procurement prices were practically on par with market prices, so that merging the two would not have much of an impact.
In some cases, the market price is even below the state procurement price, they said.
In China's northeast, for example, the government's procurement price for corn is around 1,040 yuan ($125) a tonne, while the market price is about 1,000 yuan ($120.50).
"Because of a very good harvest and previous surplus, in some regions the market price and government price are the same," one trader said, adding the reforms would hardly be noticed at the moment.
China raised purchase prices to farmers this year by about 20 percent and grain prices dropped on a healthy harvest, narrowing the state to market differential.
The central authorities buy a certain amount of grain from farmers at prices set below the market rate to ensure adequate state grain reserves.
The unification could increase price volatility in the long run, grain traders said.
"Ultimately, its going to make for more volatile prices," because government purchase prices were used to indicate the lowest levels grain prices could drop to, the Singapore trader said.
"If you take that away, then it's a bit harder to say when prices have gone low enough," he said.
All depended on the grain price direction next year, industry sources said.
If prices rose, the market would provide farmers with the incentive to plant grain. But if grain prices then plummeted on another bumper harvest, farmers might complain, sources said.
"Will they then insist on (farmers planting particular commodities), or will they say you can plant what you want," the Singapore trader said, noting that issue had not been raised.
China's lack of sophisticated agricultural futures markets -- which did not allow farmers to lock in profits -- was part of the issue, other industry sources suggested.
Most traders said further details on how the government planned to implement the new policy were needed before a final assessment of the reforms could be made.
